item.title: Meta Platforms ordered to pay $25 billion in New Mexico consumer data protection case
item.description: New Mexico accused Meta of misleading Facebook users about who could access their personal data, how the company dealt with hate speech and misinformation, and other internal policies
item.dc:creator: Livemint
item.content:encoded: A New Mexico judge has ordered Meta Platforms to pay $25 billion after a jury found that the company misled consumers about its data privacy practices, in a case stemming from allegations that millions of Facebook users' personal information was obtained without their consent, Reuters reported.Judge Francis Mathew ruled on Wednesday that a penalty exceeding $219 billion was warranted under state law but reduced the amount to $25 billion."Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the verdict.The lawsuit was filed by New Mexico's attorney general in 2021 following revelations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, had harvested personal data from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party application.The case centres on allegations that Meta misrepresented how it handled users' personal information and addressed harmful content on its platforms.Jury finds more than 43 million violationsNew Mexico accused Meta of misleading Facebook users about who could access their personal data, how the company dealt with hate speech and misinformation, and other internal policies.The state alleged that Meta knew third parties had extensive access to users' information and tolerated harmful content when doing so benefited its business.On September 25, jurors found that 26 of 29 statements made by Meta and its leadership on these issues were misleading. They determined that the company had committed more than 43 million violations of New Mexico's consumer protection laws, based on the number of Facebook users or state residents exposed to each misleading statement.State law permits penalties of up to $5,000 per violation. New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said after the verdict that the money would go to the state's school system.State sought up to $40 billion in penaltiesAt an October 1 hearing, Randi McGinn, a lawyer representing New Mexico, asked Judge Mathew to award the state between $35 billion and $40 billion.McGinn argued that the amount would be consistent with the jury's verdict and the due process protections provided by the US Constitution.Meta, however, urged the court to cap the penalties at $3.45 billion, warning that a significantly higher amount could discourage businesses from operating in the state.In court filings, the company argued that it did not sell users' personal data and that the state had failed to demonstrate that any consumer had actually been misled.The $25 billion order represents a substantial penalty, although it is below the amount sought by the state's legal team and far lower than the figure the judge said was justified under state law.Second major legal setback for Meta in New MexicoThe verdict marks the second time in six months that a Santa Fe jury has ruled against Meta in a lawsuit brought by New Mexico.In the first trial, which concluded in March, jurors found that Meta had misled users about the safety of young people on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. The jury ordered the company to pay $375 million in civil penalties.Following a second phase of that trial, a judge directed Meta to pay an additional $567 million into a New Mexico fund for teen mental health.The court also ordered the company to implement measures to protect teenage users of Facebook and Instagram in the state.The latest ruling adds to Meta's legal challenges over consumer protection, data privacy and online safety, as regulators and governments continue to scrutinise how major technology platforms handle users' information and address harmful content.

item.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, wife donate $75 million to Vanderbilt University for new design college
item.description: The new institution will be named the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design. The campus is expected to open in 2027, subject to regulatory approvals, and will build on the legacy of the California College of the Arts
item.dc:creator: Livemint
item.content:encoded: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, have donated $75 million to Vanderbilt University to establish a new college focused on art, architecture and design at its planned San Francisco campus. Announced on July 21, 2026, the contribution is intended to bring creative disciplines together with technology, engineering and entrepreneurship. According to the university, the donation has helped attract additional philanthropic commitments, taking total support for the San Francisco campus beyond $100 million. The new institution will be named the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang College of Art, Architecture and Design. The campus is expected to open in 2027, subject to regulatory approvals, and will build on the legacy of the California College of the Arts (CCA). Matching gift attracts additional contributionsThe Huang family's donation is structured as a matching gift designed to encourage other donors to support Vanderbilt's expansion in San Francisco.The university said alumni and other supporters had made additional commitments following the announcement. Early contributors include Katie and Matt Paige, Jeff and Marieke Rothschild, and Leah and Ben Spero. The fundraising effort has also received commitments from anonymous donors and members of the Bay Area's arts and creative communities.Vanderbilt said it had secured more than 40% of the funding required to fulfil the full matching commitment by December 31, 2028. The funds will support the establishment and operation of the new college, alongside other academic programmes planned for the campus.College to combine creative and technical educationThe proposed college will integrate studio practice and design laboratories with technical education, engineering and entrepreneurship. Vanderbilt plans to offer undergraduate and graduate degrees, as well as community arts programmes, pre-collegiate courses and lifelong-learning opportunities.The programmes will be subject to the necessary academic reviews and regulatory approvals.Explaining the rationale behind the contribution, Huang said in Vanderbilt's announcement: “Technology expands what we can build. Art and design determine why we build it. Together they shape civilization.”The initiative reflects the couple's stated belief that artistic creativity and design can contribute to technological progress, business innovation and the cultural development of cities.Vanderbilt expects the San Francisco campus to accommodate approximately 1,000 undergraduate and graduate students, alongside full-time faculty and staff. The project forms part of the university's broader expansion beyond its main campus in Nashville, Tennessee.Vanderbilt plans to preserve California College of the Arts legacyThe San Francisco project will build on CCA's nearly 120-year history. Vanderbilt and CCA have agreed that CCA will contribute its campus to Vanderbilt after its operations wind down, subject to customary regulatory and other transaction requirements.Vanderbilt also plans to establish the California College of the Arts Institute to preserve and extend the institution's artistic and cultural legacy.The proposed institute will include the Wattis Institute for Contemporary Arts, preserve and digitise CCA's archives, and support artists, designers, architects, curators and scholars through fellowships and residencies.The university has begun a national search for the founding dean of the new college. Its opening remains contingent on the required approvals, with the first students expected in 2027.Separate initiative supports AI and scientific research The Vanderbilt donation is separate from another philanthropic initiative involving the Huang family. In May 2026, Reuters reported that the foundation run by Jensen and Lori Huang had purchased computing time from CoreWeave and donated it to universities and nonprofit organisations for scientific and artificial intelligence research. A regulatory filing valued the donated computing resources at $108.3 million. Nvidia also planned to provide free engineering services to some recipients. CoreWeave uses Nvidia-designed graphics processing units for AI workloads. Reuters noted that Nvidia had invested $2 billion in CoreWeave and agreed to purchase $6.3 billion in cloud capacity from the company, relationships that had raised investor concerns about potential circular financing. While the computing initiative focuses on research infrastructure, the Vanderbilt contribution is aimed at creating an academic institution that connects art, design and technology.
